zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This aid supports lexical identification, not this copy's glyphs, spacing, or typeface.

lines.note: This completes Cor-/rerem from the preceding page: tears flow. The next Japanese example says that sweat flows; the page's catchword is not part of this body row.
The Portuguese translates the preceding example as the flowing of sweat, distinguishing it from the example about tears.
Nagare is the noun for a current or flow of water; the short Portuguese gloss supplies that concrete sense.

runs.text: Ir de cà pera là leua-

lines.note: Nagare ariqi describes moving here and there while carried by water. The scan supports grave accents in cà and là, rather than the draft's nasal mark and unaccented form; leua- continues on the next row.
The gloss completes being carried by water. Its Japanese example introduces something luminous upon the waves; Ficarimono belongs to the example, not to the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: ni vcabite canata conataye nagare ariqi

lines.note: The luminous object floats and drifts hither and thither. The Japanese syntax continues through the next row's final verb ending.

The example concludes with ſoro and a Taif. citation, book 26. The Portuguese translation starts with a radiance; the citation label is roman, whereas Lib. 26. and the translation are italic in the scan.

runs.text: que andaua ſobre as ondas de hũa parte pera

lines.note: The Portuguese describes the radiance moving over the waves from one place toward another, continuing the translation rather than introducing a new entry.

runs.text: outra correndo, ou leuado dagoa. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The translation completes motion carried by water. Item then introduces an additional figurative use of the same Japanese expression.

runs.text: per met. Andar de cà pera là recreandoſe.

lines.note: The figurative sense is wandering here and there for recreation, extending watery drifting to leisurely human movement.
Nagare cacari is catching on something while drifting downstream. The printed abai continues as xo without a visible end-of-line hyphen, which is not supplied editorially.

runs.text: xo ficar preſo em algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The Portuguese completes getting caught on something while carried downstream. The example begins with a reference to the water.
The Japanese example concerns snakes being swept along and briefly catching at someone's feet; febidomo and axini support the following Portuguese translation.

The example ends in the connective cacarite and cites Fox., book 2. The scan reads As co-, beginning the Portuguese word for snakes; the draft had lost the capital A and the separation after the book number.

runs.text: bras que hião correndo polla agoa a baixo fican-

lines.note: The snakes are described as travelling downstream and becoming caught. Both co-/bras and fican-/do are physical line divisions, not separate words.

runs.text: do hum pouco aferradas nos pees.

lines.note: The translation finishes by saying that the snakes caught briefly at the feet, explaining the contact implied by cacari.
Nagareide means for water or a similar substance to flow out; the conjugational forms are retained as printed rather than recast in modern spelling.

runs.text: correndo como de tanque, ou fonte.

lines.note: A tank or fountain provides the Portuguese examples of a source from which water flows out.

This entry identifies nagarenomi with yūjo and glosses it as a prostitute. Reinspection at enlargement establishes a circumflex, not a caron, in Yûgio. The usage label P. is upright in the scan and is separated from the italic Portuguese; the Japanese synonym is not an embedded Portuguese term.
Nagarevochi means falling or being knocked down and swept away; der- begins the Portuguese derrubado continued below.
The gloss completes being brought down and carried by water. The example begins with constructing a bridge, with ca-/quredomo divided at the printed line end.
The example contrasts building the bridge with its being swept away in a flood. The marked vowel in cǒzui and the divided nagarevochi- are retained from the scan.
The Japanese past form is completed by ta. The Portuguese begins the corresponding concessive statement: although they built a bridge, nevertheless something happened to it.

runs.text: no tempo da enchente cabio, & foy pella agoa

lines.note: During the flood the bridge fell and was carried away. The scan actually prints cabio with a b-shaped letter; that historical or erroneous form is preserved rather than silently replaced by caiu or cahio.
This single-word continuation completes the bridge's being carried downstream and closes the preceding example.

Nagarevxe denotes something being lost through being washed away. The second scan pass distinguishes the angular v from the draft u; the post-reading NINJAL lexical checkpoint also supports this headword identity. The cause of that loss is supplied on the following row.
The loss is explicitly attributed to a great flood, rather than to ordinary disappearance.
Nagaſarebito is an exiled or banished person; the Portuguese gives the corresponding participial noun.
Nagaſode literally denotes long sleeves, setting up the following application to religious dress.
The long-sleeved person is explained as a Buddhist cleric or religious person in Japan. The printed division Ia/pão has no visible hyphen, which is preserved.

runs.text: pão que vestem habito de mangas compridas.

lines.note: The explanation specifies robes with long sleeves. This physical continuation starts at the same inset as neighboring continuation rows; its missing indentation has been restored.
The example adds de to express being in the capacity of a Buddhist cleric; the Portuguese rendering continues below.
This completes the alternative Portuguese description as a religious person, not a separate headword.

runs.text: O andar muito tempo fora de ſua ca-

lines.note: Nagatabi is a long journey or prolonged absence from home. The Portuguese defines it by the time spent away, with ca-/ſa divided between rows.
The example combines nagatabi with the object marker and suru: to undertake a long journey or stay away from home for a long time.

runs.text: Faca larga, ou manchil da cozi-

lines.note: Nagatana is described as a broad kitchen knife or cleaver. The scan has a final l in manchil, omitted in the draft; the word for kitchen continues as cozi-/nha.
The instrument is used to cut herbs or vegetables, specifying its kitchen function rather than a weapon's use.
Nagavaqizaxi is a long wakizashi, glossed here as a long dagger; the historical romanization is kept.
Nagaxengui denotes a lengthy consultation or deliberation, another compound using the idea of length or duration.

runs.text: Chuuas do verão que durão muito em

lines.note: This noun denotes prolonged summer rain in Japan. It is distinct from the identically headed verb in the next entry.

The Portuguese says that the upper-region expression is Tçuyu, tsuyu. Cami occurs within the Portuguese explanation, and Tçuyu is the name quoted by that explanation rather than an independent example sentence.
The verb nagaxi means causing water or another liquid to flow. Its transitive force contrasts with earlier nagare entries describing the water's own movement.
The liquid gloss concludes, then an example is translated as making it rain heavily. The printed Fa/zer crosses the row boundary without a hyphen.
The heavy-rain translation is completed. Nauo naga-/ſu introduces the figurative expression of spreading a bad reputation.
The Portuguese makes this use explicitly negative: to spread a bad reputation or defame, rather than merely to make someone's name known.
With namida as object, the verb means shedding tears. No terminal punctuation is supplied beyond what is visible in the printed row.

One example means sweating. The next begins Couo vmi and continues at the top of the right column; the final i is visible and has been restored, enabling the printed expression about losing a pregnancy to be read across the column boundary.

runs.text: Mouer a molher antes de tempo.

lines.note: This completes Couo vmi nagaſu from the left column. The Portuguese describes a woman miscarrying before term; the body row is an indented continuation, not a new headword.
Another transitive use is banishment: the example says to exile a person. This explains the relation to the earlier noun for an exile, nagaſarebito.
Nagaxicaqe concerns directing flowing water toward or through a particular place; the complement is completed on the next row.
The water is made to run through some place, completing the spatial force of the compound verb.
Nagayari is a long spear; the Portuguese gives the weapon and its distinguishing length.
Nagaye denotes the pole or shaft of a cart, glossed by the historical Portuguese temão.
Nagazaiqiǒ is a prolonged stay in the capital. Miyaco is the Japanese place designation embedded in the Portuguese gloss, whose deuagar here concerns an unhurried or extended stay.
Nagazama is explained as a long window or opening; the printed initial I of Ianela is retained.
Nagazaqe denotes a drinking gathering that lasts a long time, not simply a long vessel or a quantity of liquor.
The month name is equated with the ninth month. Cuguat is a standalone Japanese synonym, and the Portuguese specifies the ninth lunar month in Japan.
Nagǒ is the adverbial long-vowel form of long. The following example applies length and breadth figuratively to one's heart or disposition.
The Japanese example urges a patient, broad disposition. Its final citation is printed as italic Mõ.; the tightly set quattofirǒ is retained rather than respaced from a modern reconstruction.

runs.text: Tendo grande, & largo coraçaõ, l, ſendo lõ-

lines.note: The Portuguese translates having a large and broad heart, alternatively being long-suffering. The abbreviated nasal spelling lõ- is continued below.
This finishes lõ-/ganime, the Portuguese adjective expressing patience or forbearance, and closes the example.
The primary gloss concerns lingering waves: nagori, alternatively nagori no nami, describes what remains after the disturbance has passed.
The waves remain disturbed after a past storm. Item introduces a metaphorical extension from these aftereffects to lingering human feeling.
The figurative gloss is saudades, longing or the sorrow of parting. The Japanese example begins nagori o oshimu, lamenting a departure.

runs.text: Ter grandes ſaudades, quando ſe hum

lines.note: The example's verb is completed by mu. The Portuguese explains strong longing or regret when someone takes leave of another person.

runs.text: deſpede dalguem. ¶ Item, per met. Ter

lines.note: The first part completes taking leave. The next figurative sense begins with Ter; despite the paper crease across its lower part, the terminal glyph is an r rather than the draft's hyphen.

runs.text: ſaudade, & lembrança dalgũa couſa a praziuel,

lines.note: This extends longing to remembrance of a pleasant thing. A crease damages the middle of a praziuel; that chosen reading follows the surviving opening and -iuel traces and the sentence, while retaining the draft's separation after a. The row's visible continuation inset is restored.

runs.text: ou gostoſa como da primauera, das flores, &c.

lines.note: Spring and flowers are the examples of delightful things remembered. The scan supports das flores, correcting the draft's badly merged and misrecognized letters.
The waves expression refers the reader back to Nagori. The italic directive is Vide, with a comma, not the draft's Vida.
Nagorivoxij is the adjective for finding a parting regrettable or feeling great longing; the Portuguese describes that emotional state.
The indented -ſa derivative names the quality or degree of the preceding feeling. It has no separate Portuguese gloss in this printed row.

The adverbial derivative is exemplified with omou, feeling longing or regret. Both occurrences visibly use v in voxǔ, so the example's draft u has been corrected without changing the historical long-vowel marks.
This gives the Portuguese translation of the preceding example: to feel longing or the sorrow associated with parting.
Nagorivoximi names the feeling of regretting a departure. The scan supports v rather than the draft's r in the headword, and g rather than ç in the start of the example.

The example describes holding a drinking gathering in the spirit of a fond farewell. The creased Portuguese word is read bebere-, completed by te below; the surviving letters and the corresponding drinking example support this repair.
The gathering is held with affection and the feeling of parting. The row completes beberete and the translation of the farewell example.

Nagoyacana means quiet or tranquil. A diagonal crease obscures part of quieta, but the surviving qui- and final -ta, the alternative tranquila, and the next row's weather example support the chosen reading in place of the corrupted draft.

The Japanese says that the weather is calm. The crease crosses the middle of nagoyacani, but the remaining strokes and adjacent forms support it; the Portuguese is read otempo, retaining its tightly set join rather than introducing an unsupported space.
The Portuguese completes the description of calm, serene weather. The first letter of ſereno is the printed long s, not j; the row is visibly inset like the surrounding continuations.
This separate headword identifies the adverbial form of nagoyacana, already illustrated in the preceding weather sentence.
Nague is the verb to throw or cast. Its historical paradigm is preserved, and the entry proceeds to examples involving the whole body.
The first example literally casts the whole body to the ground. The Portuguese translates throwing oneself down and leaves the accompanying emotion to the next row.
The action is motivated by grief or another strong emotion. The next example begins mi o na-/guru, casting one's own body.

runs.text: Botarſe, ou afogarſe no mar, ou rio.

lines.note: The second example is glossed as throwing oneself into, or drowning in, the sea or a river; this is the dictionary's historical usage illustration.
Nagueague means lifting and throwing upward. The scan visibly has double r in arreme-, restoring a consonant lost in the draft without modernizing the rest of the spelling.
The example describes grasping firmly and throwing up onto a bank or higher ground. The printed long-vowel mark in tçucǒde is retained.
The Japanese action is completed by nague agueta. The citation label reads Feiq., book 4, rather than Fciq.; the Portuguese then begins the act of gripping firmly.

runs.text: rando fortemente com as mãos o arremeſou em

lines.note: The translation describes grasping firmly with the hands and throwing the object upward, continuing Afer-/rando across the physical rows.

runs.text: cima da barroca, ou terra alta.

lines.note: The destination is the top of a bank or other high ground, completing the upward direction expressed in the compound verb.
Naguecaqe is glossed as throwing or casting, a separate compound from the upward-throwing verb above.

runs.text: Couſa penoſa, ou que cauſa dor.

lines.note: Naguecaxij is something lamentable, grievous, or causing pain. Its meaning is distinct from the preceding throwing verbs despite the neighboring alphabetical spelling.
The indented -ſa derivative names the grievousness or degree of sorrow associated with naguecaxij; no additional gloss is printed.
This is the adverbial long-vowel derivative of the same adjective, again listed without an independent Portuguese definition.
Naguecayexi means throwing back or throwing again. The Portuguese prints Tornar with both n and r, correcting the draft's Torar; the catchword below is separate page furniture.

The faint catchword is read Nague.; its terminal mark is weak, so the draft's period is retained rather than resolved as a hyphen. This material is separate from the signature and the final body entry.
